drivingQuestion: Is the mishna's ruling that one redeems from the buyer's son not self-evident?
outcomeNote: The redundancy charge is answered exactly as in the previous clause, from ״והיתה גאולתו״ — מכל מקום.

segments.he: מֵת הַלּוֹקֵחַ יִגְאַל מִיָּד בְּנוֹ וְכוּ׳. פְּשִׁיטָא! מַהוּ דְּתֵימָא: ״לַקּוֹנֶה אוֹתוֹ״ אָמַר רַחֲמָנָא, וְהָא לָא קְנָה — קָא מַשְׁמַע לַן: ״וְהָיְתָה גְּאֻלָּתוֹ״ מִכׇּל מָקוֹם.
segments.en: The mishna further teaches: If «the buyer died,» the seller «may redeem» the house «from the possession of» the buyer’s «son.» The Gemara asks: This, too, is «obvious.» The Gemara responds: «Lest you say» that «the Merciful One states:» “Then the house that is in the walled city shall stand in possession «of the one who bought it» in perpetuity” (Leviticus 25:30), «and» as «this» son did «not buy» the house, the buyer cannot redeem it from him; therefore, the previous verse «teaches us: “He shall have the right of redemption,”» indicating that this right applies «in any case,» even from the buyer’s son.
